new_statements.quote: In Bwe, a central Karen dialect which has three tones — high level, mid level, low level, — we come across an interesting use of tonal variation in compounding which may be referred to as tonal dissimilation, since in the formation of compounds there appears to be a deliberate variation of the tones of the elements as isolates, particularly when these have the same tone. [...] [fn. 10:] The notation of the Bwe Tones is as follows:— high level [ˊa], mid level [¯a], low level [ˎa]. Short unstressed syllables are not marked as bearing tone, since pitch is not contrastive on such syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bwe (Western Bwe/Blimaw) is a three-level-tone language in which only stressed (major, full) syllables bear contrastive tone; short unstressed syllables have no contrastive pitch. The positional rule is stated only second-hand from the introduction to Henderson 1997 (by David Solnit): a word has one stressed major syllable; unstressed minor (prefix) syllables, with schwa or reduced vowel, always precede it and carry no distinct tone; unstressed suffix syllables follow it and copy its tone. So stress falls on the root/major syllable, i.e. the last full syllable of a sesquisyllabic word (prefix + root), with any suffix unstressed (Namkung 1996: 158-159; Naw Hsar Shee 2008: 20). Compounds of full syllables are handled tonally (dissimilation 'word-intonation' patterns high-low / low-high), and no open source states which element of a compound is stressed; Henderson 1961 (p. 69) apparently compares Bwe compounds to the single strong stress of English 'blackbird' but could not be read.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Henderson 1967 gives no exceptions. Second-hand from Henderson 1997 via Namkung 1996 p. 159: an unstressed suffix takes the tone of the preceding stressed syllable except that after a high-tone syllable a suffix with voiced initial is mid tone; schwa of an unstressed prefix may assimilate to the following stressed vowel. For the sister language Geba, Naw Hsar Shee 2008 p. 21 notes that grammatical particles vary in stress with phrasal intonation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (prefix + root (+ suffix) structures and compounds); Henderson's remark is a transcription convention in a paper on grammatical tone, based on her Western Bwe (Blimaw, Mehbyu area) field data; the second-hand rule from Henderson 1997/Namkung 1996 refers to citation forms. Henderson 1979 uses 'word-intonation' for tonal dissimilation across the syllables of disyllabic words rather than stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand data are Henderson's Western Bwe, Blimaw dialect, Mehbyu area (Henderson 1979 §1.3; 1985 p. 55); Glottolog maps Henderson 1997 'Western Bwe' to bwek1238 [bwe]. Namkung 1996 adds a second entry for Chitabu-village Bwe from Weidert 1987. Do not confuse with Shintani 2017 'The Blimaw language', which hh.bib notes is Mobwa Karen [jkm], not Henderson's Bwe. Naw Hsar Shee 2008 describes the sister language Geba Karen [kvq] (Glottolog Geba-Bwe subgroup geba1236); its Bwe remarks (p. 20) are a second-hand summary of Henderson 1997.

sources.note: Section 4.5 'In Bwe Karen' (p. 175): Bwe is a three-tone (high/mid/low level) central Karen dialect; footnote 10 states that short unstressed syllables are not marked as bearing tone because pitch is not contrastive on them; compounds show tonal dissimilation ('word-intonation'), no positional stress rule given. First-hand (Henderson's own field data).

For the prefix forms there are no distinctions in tone, but the suffixes take the tone of the immediately preceding syllable, if the suffix has a voiced initial' (Henderson 1997: front matter). sources.citation: Henderson, E. J. A. 1979. Bwe Karen as a two-tone language? An enquiry into the interrelations of pitch, tone and initial consonant. In Nguyen Dang Liem (ed.), South-East Asian linguistic studies vol. 3, 301-335. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics C-45. DOI 10.15144/PL-C45.301.
sources.note: No use of the word stress. §2.2: all Western Bwe (Blimaw) syllables are CV, no finals; §2.3 distinguishes full 'normal' monosyllabic words from syllables found only as the first (bound) syllable of disyllabic/polysyllabic words; §2.1, §3(e): disyllables frequently carry a 'word-intonation pattern' of tonal dissimilation (high-low or low-high, e.g. ka1me3 'tail', ka1 = 'bottom'). Purely a pitch/tone study.
